raw_text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader||TRIGONOMETRY|281}}</noinclude>27. We shall now obtain expressions for <math>\sin x</math> and <math>\cos x</math> as infinite products of rational factors. We have
{{EB1911 Shoulder Heading|Factorization of Sine and Cosine.}}
{{block center|<math>\sin x = 2\sin\frac{x}{2}\cdot\sin\frac{x+\pi}{2} = 2^3\sin\frac{x}{4}\cdot\sin\frac{x+\pi}{4}</math>}}
{{block center|<math>\sin\frac{x+2\pi}{4}\cdot\sin\frac{x+3\pi}{4}</math>;}}
proceeding continually in this way with each factor, we obtain
{{block center|<math>\sin x = 2^{n-1}\sin\frac{x}{n}\cdot\sin\frac{x+\pi}{n}\cdot\sin\frac{x+2\pi}{n}\dots\sin\frac{x+\overline{n-1}\pi}{n}</math>,}}
where <math>n</math> is any positive integral power of 2. Now
{{block center|<math>\sin\frac{x+r\pi}{n}\cdot\sin\frac{x+n-r\pi}{n} = \sin\frac{x+r\pi}{n}\cdot\sin\frac{\overline{r\pi-x}}{n} = \sin^2\frac{r\pi}{n}-\sin^2\frac{x}{n}</math>,}}
{{block center|and <math>\sin\frac{x+\tfrac{1}{2}n\pi}{n} = \cos\frac{x}{n}</math>.}}
Hence the above may be written
{{block center|<math>\sin x = 2^{n-1}\sin\frac{x}{n}\left(\sin^2\frac{\pi}{n}-\sin^2\frac{x}{n}\right)\left(\sin^2\frac{2\pi}{n}-\sin^2\frac{x}{n}\right)\dots</math>}}
{{block center|<math>\left(\sin^2\frac{k\pi}{n}-\sin^2\frac{x}{n}\right)\cos\frac{x}{n}</math>,}}
where <math>k = \tfrac{1}{2}n = 1</math>. Let <math>x</math> be indefinitely small, then we have
{{block center|<math>1 = \frac{2^{n-1}}{n}\sin^2\frac{\pi}{n}\sin^2\frac{2\pi}{n}\dots\sin^2\frac{k\pi}{n}</math>;}}
hence
{{block center|<math>\sin x = n\sin\frac{x}{n}\cos\frac{x}{n}\left(1-\frac{\sin^2 x/n}{\sin^2\pi/n}\right)\left(1-\frac{\sin^2 x/n}{\sin^2 2\pi/n}\right)\dots\left(1-\frac{\sin^2 x/n}{\sin^2 k\pi/n}\right)</math>.}}
We may write this
{{block center|<math>\sin x = n\sin\frac{x}{n}\cos\frac{x}{n}\left(1-\frac{\sin^2 x/n}{\sin^2\pi/n}\right)\dots\left(1-\frac{\sin^2 x/n}{\sin^2 m\pi/n}\right)R</math>,}}
where <math>R</math> denotes the product
{{block center|<math>\left(1-\frac{\sin^2 x/n}{\sin^2\overline{m+1}\pi/n}\right)\left(1-\frac{\sin^2 x/n}{\sin^2\overline{m+2}\pi/n}\right)\dots\left(1-\frac{\sin^2 x/n}{\sin^2 k\pi/n}\right)</math>,}}
and <math>m</math> is any fixed integer independent of <math>n</math>. It is necessary, when we make <math>n</math> infinite, to determine the limiting value of the quantity <math>R</math>; then, since the limit of <math>\frac{\sin x}{n\sin x/n\cos x/n}</math> is <math>\frac{\sin x}{x}</math>, and that of <math>\frac{\sin m\pi/n}{m\pi/n}</math> is unity, we have
{{block center|<math>\frac{\sin x}{x} = \left(1-\frac{x^2}{\pi^2}\right)\left(1-\frac{x^2}{2^2\pi^2}\right)\dots\left(1-\frac{x^2}{m^2\pi^2}\right)\lim_{m=\infty}\text{R}</math>.}}
The modulus of <math>R-1</math> is less than
{{block center|<math>\left(1+\frac{\rho^2}{\sin^2\overline{m+1}\pi/n}\right)\left(1+\frac{\rho^2}{\sin^2\overline{m+2}\pi/n}\right)\dots\left(1+\frac{\rho^2}{\sin^2 k\pi/n}\right)-1</math>,}}

{{smaller block|where <math>\rho = \text{mod.}\ \sin x/n</math>. Now <math>e^{A\rho^2} > 1+A\rho^2</math>, if <math>A</math> is positive; hence <math>\text{mod.}\ (R-1)</math> is less than <math>\text{exp.}\ \{\rho^2(\text{cosec}^2\,\overline{m+1}\pi/n+\dots+\text{cosec}^2\,k\pi/n)-1</math>, or than <math>\text{exp.}\ \tfrac{1}{4}\rho^2n^2\{1/(m+1)^2+\dots+1/k^2\}-1</math>, or than <math>\text{exp.}\ \{\rho^2n^2/4m^2\}-1</math>. Now <math>\rho^2 = \sin^2\alpha/n.\cosh^2\beta/n+\cos^2\alpha/n.\sinh^2\beta/n</math>, if <math>x = \alpha+i\beta</math>; or <math>\rho^2 = \sin^2\alpha/n+\sinh^2\beta/n</math>. Hence <math>\lim_{n=\infty}\rho^2n^2 = \alpha^2+\beta^2</math>, <math>\lim_{n=\infty}\rho n = \text{mod.}\ x</math>. It follows that <math>\text{mod.}_{n=\infty}\ (R-1)</math> is between 0 and <math>\text{exp.}\ \{(\text{mod.}\ 4)^2/xm^2\}-1</math>, and the latter may be made arbitrarily small by taking <math>m</math> large enough. It has now been shown that <math>\sin x = x(1-x^2/\pi^2)(1-x^2/2^2\pi^2)\dots(1-x^2/m^2\pi^2)(1+\epsilon_m)</math>, where <math>\text{mod.}\ \epsilon_m</math> decreases indefinitely as <math>m</math> is increased indefinitely. When <math>m</math> is indefinitely increased this becomes
{{block center|<math>\sin x = x\left(1-\frac{x^2}{\pi^2}\right)\left(1-\frac{x^2}{2^2\pi^2}\right)\dots = x\overset{n=\infty}{\underset{n=1}{P}}\left(1-\frac{x^2}{n^2\pi^2}\right)</math>. (25)}}}}

This has been shown to hold for any real or complex value of <math>x</math>. The expression for <math>\cos x</math> in factors may be found in a similar manner by means of the equation <math>\cos x = 2\sin\frac{\pi-2x}{4}\cos\frac{3\pi-2x}{4}</math>, or may be deduced thus
{{block center|<math>\cos x = \frac{\sin 2x}{2\sin x} = \frac{P\left(1-\frac{4x^2}{n^2\pi^2}\right)}{P\left(1-\frac{x^2}{n^2\pi^2}\right)} = \left(1-\frac{4x^2}{\pi^2}\right)\left(1-\frac{4x^2}{3^2\pi^2}\right)\left(1-\frac{4x^2}{5^2\pi^2}\right)\dots</math>}}
{{block center|<math>= \overset{n=\infty}{\underset{n=0}{P}}\left(1-\frac{4x^2}{(2n+1)^2\pi^2}\right)</math>. (26)}}
If we change <math>x</math> into <math>\iota x</math>, we have the formulae for <math>\sinh x</math>, <math>\cosh x</math> as infinite products—
{{block center|<math>\sinh x = x\overset{n=\infty}{\underset{n=0}{P}}\left(1+\frac{x^2}{n^2\pi^2}\right),\quad \cosh x = \overset{n=\infty}{\underset{n=0}{P}}\left(1+\frac{4x^2}{(2n+1)^2\pi^2}\right)</math>.}}

{{smaller block|In the formula for sin <math>x</math> as an infinite product put <math>x=\tfrac{1}{2}\pi</math>, we then get <math>1=\frac{\pi}{2}\cdot\frac{1\cdot3\cdot3\cdot5\cdot5\cdot\dots}{2.2.4.4.6\dots}</math>; if we stop after <math>2n</math> factors in the numerator and denominator, we obtain the approximate equation
{{block center|<math>1=\frac{\pi}{2}\frac{1^2.3^2.5^2\dots(2n-1)^2}{2^2.4^2.6^2\dots(2n)^2}.(2n+1)</math>}}
or <math>\frac{2.4.6\dots 2n}{1.3.5\dots 2n-1}=\sqrt{n\pi}</math>, where <math>n</math> is a large integer. This expression was obtained in a quite different manner by Wallis (''Arithmetica infinitorum'', vol. i. of ''Opp.'').}}

{{smaller block|28. We have
{{EB1911 Shoulder Heading|Series for Cot, Cosec, Tan and Sec.}}
{{block center|<math>\frac{\sin(x+y)}{\sin x}=\frac{(x+y)P\left(1+\frac{x+y}{n\pi}\right)}{xP\left(1+\frac{x}{n\pi}\right)},</math>}}
or <math>\cos y+\sin y\cot x</math>
{{block center|<math>=\left(1+\frac{y}{x}\right)\left(1+\frac{y}{x+\pi}\right)\left(1+\frac{y}{x-\pi}\right)\left(1+\frac{y}{x+2\pi}\right)\left(1+\frac{y}{x-2\pi}\right)\dots</math>}}
Equating the coefficients of the first power of <math>y</math> on both sides we obtain the series
{{block center|<math>\cot x=\frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{x+\pi}+\frac{1}{x-\pi}+\frac{1}{x+2\pi}+\frac{1}{x-2\pi}+\dots</math> (27)}}
From this we may deduce a corresponding series for cosec <math>x</math>, for, since <math>\operatorname{cosec} x=\cot\tfrac{1}{2}x-\cot x</math>, we obtain
{{block center|<math>\operatorname{cosec} x=\frac{1}{x}-\frac{1}{x+\pi}-\frac{1}{x-\pi}+\frac{1}{x+2\pi}+\frac{1}{x-2\pi}-\frac{1}{x+3\pi}-\frac{1}{x-3\pi}+\dots</math> (28)}}
By resolving <math>\frac{\cos(x+y)}{\cos x}</math> into factors we should obtain in a similar manner the series
{{block center|<math>\tan x=\frac{2}{\pi-2x}-\frac{2}{\pi+2x}+\frac{2}{3\pi-2x}-\frac{2}{3\pi+2x}+\frac{2}{5\pi-2x}-\frac{2}{5\pi+2x}+\dots,</math> (29)}}
and thence
{{block center|<math>\sec x=\tan\left(\frac{\pi}{4}+\frac{x}{2}\right)-\tan x=\frac{2}{\pi-2x}+\frac{2}{\pi+2x}-\frac{2}{3\pi-2x}-\frac{2}{3\pi+2x}+\dots.</math>(30)}}
These four formulae may also be derived from the product formulae for sin <math>x</math> and cos <math>x</math> by taking logarithms and then differentiating. Glaisher has proved them by resolving the expressions for <math>\cos x/\sin x</math> and <math>1/\sin x</math> ... as products into partial fractions (see ''Quart. Journ. Math.'', vol. xvii.). The series for cot <math>x</math> may also be obtained by a continued use of the equation <math>\cot x=\tfrac{1}{2}\{\cot\tfrac{1}{2}x+\cot\tfrac{1}{2}(x+\pi)\}</math> (see a paper by Dr Schröter in Schlömilch's ''Zeitschrift'', vol. xiii.).}}

{{smaller block|Various series for <math>\pi</math> may be derived from the series (27), (28), (29), (30), and from the series obtained by differentiating them one or more times. For example, in the formulae (27) and (28), by putting <math>x=\pi/n</math> we get
{{EB1911 Shoulder Heading|Series for π derived from Series for Cot and Cosec.}}
{{block center|<math>\pi=n\tan\frac{\pi}{n}\left\{1-\frac{1}{n-1}+\frac{1}{n+1}-\frac{1}{2n-1}+\frac{1}{2n+1}\dots\right\},</math>}}
{{block center|<math>\pi=n\sin\frac{\pi}{n}\left\{1+\frac{1}{n-1}-\frac{1}{n+1}-\frac{1}{2n-1}+\frac{1}{2n+1}\dots\right\};</math>}}
If we put <math>n=3</math>, these become
{{block center|<math>\pi=3\sqrt{3}\left(1-\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{5}+\frac{1}{7}-\frac{1}{8}+\dots\right),</math>}}
{{block center|<math>\pi=\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}\left(1+\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{5}+\frac{1}{7}+\frac{1}{8}\dots\right).</math>}}
By differentiating (27) we get
{{block center|<math>\operatorname{cosec}^2 x=\frac{1}{x^2}+\frac{1}{(x+\pi)^2}+\frac{1}{(x-\pi)^2}+\frac{1}{(x+2\pi)^2}+\frac{1}{(x-2\pi)^2}+\dots;</math>}}
put <math>x=\frac{\pi}{6}</math>, and we get <math>\pi^2=9\left\{1+\frac{1}{5^2}+\frac{1}{7^2}+\frac{1}{11^2}+\dots\right\}</math>.
These series, among others, were given by Glaisher (''Quart. Journ. Math.'' vol. xii.).}}

{{smaller block|29. We have <math>\sinh\pi x=\pi xP\left(1+\frac{x^2}{n^2}\right)</math>, <math>\cosh\pi x=P\left(1+\frac{x^2}{(2n+1)^2}\right)</math>; if we differentiate these formulae after taking logarithms we obtain the series
{{EB1911 Shoulder Heading|Sums of Certain Series.}}
{{block center|<math>\frac{\pi}{2x}\coth\pi x-\frac{1}{2x^2}=\frac{1}{1^2+x^2}+\frac{1}{2^2+x^2}+\frac{1}{3^2+x^2}+\dots,</math>}}
{{block center|<math>\frac{\pi}{2x}\tanh\pi x=\frac{1}{1^2+x^2}+\frac{1}{3^2+x^2}+\frac{1}{5^2+x^2}+\dots</math>}}
These series were given by Kummer (in ''Crelle's Journ.'' vol. xvii.) The sum of the more general series <math>\frac{1}{1^{2n}+x^{2n}}+\frac{1}{2^{2n}+x^{2n}}+\frac{1}{3^{2n}+x^{2n}}+\dots</math>, has been found by Glaisher (''Proc. Lond. Math. Soc.'', vol. vii.)}}
